concept.name: Endogeneity
concept.definition: The failure of the exogeneity condition E[epsilon | X] = 0 in a regression, i.e., a regressor correlated with the error term, arising from omitted variables, simultaneity (reverse causation), or measurement error. It renders OLS estimates biased and inconsistent.
concept.intuition: The regressor and the leftover noise are tangled together, so the coefficient absorbs part of the noise's influence and no longer isolates the variable's own effect.
concept.mechanics: Sources include omitted variables correlated with included regressors, simultaneous determination of y and x, and errors-in-variables (attenuation bias). Diagnosis uses Durbin-Wu-Hausman tests comparing OLS to IV estimates; remedies include instrumental variables, natural experiments, fixed effects, or control functions.
concept.formula: In y = beta x + epsilon, endogeneity means Cov(x, epsilon) != 0, so plim beta_hat_OLS = beta + Cov(x, epsilon)/Var(x) != beta.
concept.failure_modes: Endogeneity cannot be detected from the regression output alone: it is a property of the data-generating process, so asserting exogeneity requires external argument. IV fixes are only as good as the instruments.
concept.misconceptions: That adding more controls always reduces endogeneity: controlling for variables that are themselves outcomes of x or of the error (bad controls, colliders) can create bias rather than remove it.
concept.example: Regressing asset returns on fund flows is contaminated because flows respond to past and anticipated returns, so flow is endogenous and the price-impact coefficient mixes in reverse causality.
